and an invented fact is indistinguishable from an established one the moment it is on
the page.

This scene opens on the locked study where Evelyn Crane was found. Assemble the packet and return its path.

Target length: about 700 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

When a well-locked study yields Evelyn Crane's body and a stopped pocket watch, detective-narrator Aldo March must unpick a mechanical trick, a neighbour's machine-smithing, and a ledger of motives to prove a murder that was meant to look impossible.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-aldo: Aldo March — first-person narrator and private investigator in his late thirties, dry, observant, morally impatient; intelligent but not infallible.
- char-evelyn: Evelyn Crane — the victim, a forthright, solitary woman in her fifties who collected antiques and kept meticulous ledgers.
- char-henry: Henry Crane — Evelyn's husband, a reserved retired engineer with a brittle temper and a plausible public grief.
- char-marta: Marta Reyes — long-serving housekeeper to the Cranes, practical, protective of the household and quick with a sharp observation.
- char-derek: Derek Lyle — next-door neighbor, an inventive clock- and small-machinery maker who repairs radiators and makes odd brass contraptions in his shed.
- insp-rao: Inspector Rao — official investigating officer, procedural, careful to keep the record straight, sceptical of private detectives but cooperative.
- loc-crane: Crane Manor — an old three-storey town house with stiff carpets, a coal cellar and a warren of service passages.
- loc-study: The study — Evelyn's locked room on the ground floor: heavy oak door with inside deadbolt, tall fireplace, sash window, low strip of floor near the mantel that conceals a narrow cavity.
- loc-garden: The narrow rear garden between the Cranes' house and Derek's shed; grass, an old coal chute hatch, and a low boundary wall.
- loc-cellar: Coal cellar and service void beneath the study — cramped, coal-smeared, with access from the garden via an old hatch used for deliveries.
- obj-study-door: Heavy oak door of the study fitted with an interior deadbolt and an old brass escutcheon; locked from the inside when the body was found.
- obj-study-window: Sash window in the study, latched and showing no signs of external tampering; the sill bears faint gardener's pollen.
- obj-watch: An engraved antique pocket watch found beneath Evelyn's hand; its hands stopped at 9:07 and its case bears a hairline puncture and faint oil residue.
- obj-note: A small folded scrap of paper clenched in Evelyn's fingers with a two-line cipher and, on the outside, a trace of red sealing-wax.
- obj-ashtray: A crystal ashtray on the desk holding three cigarette butts of an uncommon coarse brand not usually smoked in the house.
- obj-wax: A small flake of red sealing-wax found near the mantel; it matches the residue on the note and the crate-seal impression on a label later found in Derek's shed.
- obj-clockwork: A small clockwork mechanism — brass plates, a wound mainspring and a cam-mounted push-rod — discovered hidden under the hearth; stained with the same oil as the watch.
- obj-ladder: A lightweight aluminium extension ladder leaning against the boundary wall in the garden the morning after the murder; one rung has fresh scraping consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch.
- obj-coal-hatch: The external coal chute hatch in the garden leading to the cellar beneath the study; its bolt shows recent abrasion and coal dust on the latch.
- obj-filing-mark: A tiny, distinctive filing nick on a brass plate from the clockwork — a maker's tic that Aldo recognises from Derek's workbench.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural solutions or unexplained actions; the locked-room must be resolved by physical mechanism, misdirection, or human action consistent with the environment.
- All clues relied on in the solution must be introduced to the reader (or the narrator) before the reveal scene and have identifiable provenance.
- Times, locations and physical traces must be internally consistent (the watch's stopped time, hatch abrasions, ladder marks, oil stains and filing nick must align with the clockwork reconstruction).
- Forensic detail may be stylised but must not violate basic plausibility (no instantaneous chemical transformations, no impossible mechanical feats).
- The narrator (Aldo) is a competent, essentially reliable detective; he may withhold interpretation but not facts.
- No later scene may introduce new characters, locations, or significant objects not listed above without explicitly adding them to the index with provenance.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

content.text:
People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.

"Bag it and photograph it," I said. "Label the cavity." Rao's pen made the concession of the official record and the room rearranged itself into objects to be logged.

I handled the piece with gloved care. The oil on its plates matched the smudge on the watch-case Clara—no, Evelyn—had been holding. (Names have a way of slipping in a room like this; I corrected myself quietly.) That shared oil made a mechanical link I could not yet account for. One brass plate bore a tiny filing nick, a maker's tic I had seen on pieces worked at Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition points you toward questions; it is not accusation.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

While Rao began the inventory I went through them one by one.

"Where were you at nine?" I asked Henry.

"In the morning room — same chair by the hearth; I was reading the paper. Ask Marta; she brought my tea." He glanced to Marta; his throat tightened.

"Did you see him then?" I asked Marta.

"I was serving breakfast. I put his tea down in the kitchen at nine; he wasn't in the morning room." She pressed her lips and, under her breath, muttered, "She said he'd taken money."

"And you?" I looked at Derek.

"In the shed. Been filing brass all morning — had a stubborn plate this morning." He looked at the disassembled clockwork and his hand went to his shirt as if for a tool. When I said the word "ledger" his jaw flicked; the room took the motion in silence.

There. Henry's chair and Marta's kitchen time could not both be true. Marta's mutter about money gave me the small, sharp motive I needed to file separately: accusation without a page. Derek placed himself with brass and tools and gave me the one concrete connection to the mechanism beyond my recognition.

There were loose motives in the house like pages waiting to be balanced: Evelyn's ledger was spoken of in low tones, overdue accounts hinted at, and a recent angry exchange was referred to without quotation. I had not been shown specific entries, nor the exact text of that conversation, but Marta's aside and the tension between Henry and Marta were concrete enough to be worth following.

The oil smelled of small machines: industry in a house that preferred its mechanisms tucked away. It sat in the hearth, in the cavity and on the watch like a repeated signature. Noticing that the oil had crept into the mechanism's creases and into the punctured watch-case suggested they had been in contact with the same source rather than merely the same room.

Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.

Marta stood with the posture of someone who has kept a household's wrongs in order; Henry's hands were clenched in his pockets; Derek's forearms carried the permanent thumb-gouge of someone at a bench. The ladder and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for now, the cleanest things in the narrative: they were the sort of traces you could measure without pleading a story into them.

When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.

### recent-scene-s-001  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

s-001, 2 scene(s) before this one:

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

./novel/outline/logline.md:1:When a well-locked study yields Evelyn Crane's body and a stopped pocket watch, detective-narrator Aldo March must unpick a mechanical trick, a neighbour's machine-smithing, and a ledger of motives to prove a murder that was meant to look impossible.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md:1:I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md:21:"In the shed. Been filing brass all morning — had a stubborn plate this morning." He looked at the disassembled clockwork and his hand went to his shirt as if for a tool. When I said the word "ledger" his jaw flicked; the room took the motion in silence.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md:25:There were loose motives in the house like pages waiting to be balanced: Evelyn's ledger was spoken of in low tones, overdue accounts hinted at, and a recent angry exchange was referred to without quotation. I had not been shown specific entries, nor the exact text of that conversation, but Marta's aside and the tension between Henry and Marta were concrete enough to be worth following.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md:29:Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md:33:When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md:13:Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

content.text:
I started where the smell was strongest and worked outwards. Inspector Rao and I prised up the study's low hearth strip; it came away complaining. Behind it was a narrow pocket, black with old soot and the kind of neatness houses give to things they'd rather forget. Nestled there was a compact clockwork — tiny plates of brass, a wound spring and a cam-driven push-rod — its surfaces darkened where oil had pooled.

"Bag it and photograph it," I said. "Label the cavity." Rao's pen made the concession of the official record and the room rearranged itself into objects to be logged.

I handled the piece with gloved care. The oil on its plates matched the smudge on the watch-case Clara—no, Evelyn—had been holding. (Names have a way of slipping in a room like this; I corrected myself quietly.) That shared oil made a mechanical link I could not yet account for. One brass plate bore a tiny filing nick, a maker's tic I had seen on pieces worked at Derek Lyle's bench. Recognition points you toward questions; it is not accusation.

After the hearth we moved into the garden. An aluminium extension ladder leaned against the boundary wall; one rung carried a fresh scrape consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch. The external coal chute hatch's bolt showed recent abrasion and coal dust in the latch groove.

While Rao began the inventory I went through them one by one.

"Where were you at nine?" I asked Henry.

"In the morning room — same chair by the hearth; I was reading the paper. Ask Marta; she brought my tea." He glanced to Marta; his throat tightened.

"Did you see him then?" I asked Marta.

"I was serving breakfast. I put his tea down in the kitchen at nine; he wasn't in the morning room." She pressed her lips and, under her breath, muttered, "She said he'd taken money."

"And you?" I looked at Derek.

"In the shed. Been filing brass all morning — had a stubborn plate this morning." He looked at the disassembled clockwork and his hand went to his shirt as if for a tool. When I said the word "ledger" his jaw flicked; the room took the motion in silence.

There. Henry's chair and Marta's kitchen time could not both be true. Marta's mutter about money gave me the small, sharp motive I needed to file separately: accusation without a page. Derek placed himself with brass and tools and gave me the one concrete connection to the mechanism beyond my recognition.

There were loose motives in the house like pages waiting to be balanced: Evelyn's ledger was spoken of in low tones, overdue accounts hinted at, and a recent angry exchange was referred to without quotation. I had not been shown specific entries, nor the exact text of that conversation, but Marta's aside and the tension between Henry and Marta were concrete enough to be worth following.

The oil smelled of small machines: industry in a house that preferred its mechanisms tucked away. It sat in the hearth, in the cavity and on the watch like a repeated signature. Noticing that the oil had crept into the mechanism's creases and into the punctured watch-case suggested they had been in contact with the same source rather than merely the same room.

Rao was methodical, and he would write where the device had been found. What I did not have was the forensic line that tells you exactly where the oil took hold — mortar, lead hearth, the joining timbers — a small omission that could matter if somebody later argued whether the device had been placed in the cavity or had been there long enough to leave transfer stains. I put a note against the entry for later.

Marta stood with the posture of someone who has kept a household's wrongs in order; Henry's hands were clenched in his pockets; Derek's forearms carried the permanent thumb-gouge of someone at a bench. The ladder and the scuffed bolt on the coal-hatch were, for now, the cleanest things in the narrative: they were the sort of traces you could measure without pleading a story into them.

When Rao moved away to brief his sergeant, I closed my notebook and set a small list against the case: secure and photograph the clockwork, photograph the hatch and ladder, get access to Derek's bench and request a copy of Evelyn's ledger. Concrete verbs, enough to start the work. I folded the book and went back inside.

The study itself was obediently quiet. The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill bore faint gardener's pollen. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

On the desk a crystal ashtray held three cigarette butts of an uncommon coarse brand not usually smoked in the house. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like something wound too tightly and then let go. I made a point of breathing around it; smells have a way of telling the order of events better than people do.

Marta's protectiveness showed in the way she interrupted anyone who moved toward the desk, her voice low and immediate. Derek's presence was odd; he kept to the doorway as if waiting for permission to be useful.

Inspector Rao and I traded the necessary courtesies and left the room in each other's hands—his in the legal sense, mine more practical. The study would be sealed again and logged; evidence would be photographed and catalogued. ### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.

People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.
